newsitem.title: USA: Clinton decides to renew China's MFN trade status.
newsitem.headline: Clinton decides to renew China's MFN trade status.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday said he planned to renew most favoured nation trade status (MFN) for China, firing the opening shot in what is expected to be a new foreign policy battle with Congress.

Speaking to businessmen, Clinton said he had decided to accord China what amounts to normal trade tariff status for the coming year despite his disagreements with Beijing on many issues, notably its human rights record.
"Our broad policy is engagement. That doesn't mean that we win every point, but it means we work together when we can and we're honest in our disagreements when they exist," he said.
"I believe if we were to revoke normal trade status it would cut off our contact with the Chinese people and undermine our influence with the Chinese government."

MFN gives China the normal trade status the United States accords all but six nations: Afghanistan, Cuba, Laos, North Korea, Serbia and Vietnam. Iran, Iraq and Libya technically enjoy MFN status but are subject to separate trade embargoes.

The move to renew China's MFN status, an annual decision that every president has made since 1980, was expected to be controversial in Congress, where some legislators have already said they will seek to reverse the decision.

Under the law, Clinton must formally inform Congress of his decision by June 3. The House of Representatives and the Senate, to overturn the decision, have until Aug. 31 to pass a joint resolution disapproving it.
If Clinton were to veto such a resolution, both chambers would then have to muster a two-thirds majority to override his veto and prevail in the annual policy battle.

Officials and private analysts are reasonably confident Clinton can prevent his opponents from mustering the votes needed to override the MFN decision, although White House officials declined to predict the administration's chances.
Clinton, who has agreed to a summit with Chinese President Jiang Zemin later this year, has worked hard to improve ties with Beijing over the past two years.
But China's human rights record, its sale of missiles and technology to regions that are becoming unstable and its huge trade surplus with the United States remain problems.
Many in the United States -- including U.S. officials, lawmakers and businessmen -- are also concerned about the future of Hong Kong when control of the British colony reverts to Beijing on July 1.

Defending his decision, Clinton argued that the United States had an interest in China's political and economic reform and would have little sway over the country if it were to curtail its trade relationship.

"The United States has a huge stake in the continued emergence of China in a way that is open economically and stable politically," he said. "Of course we hope that it will come to respect human rights more and the rule of law more."

Clinton argued that the policy of engagement with China had already paid some dividends, saying the two countries had worked together on extending the nuclear non-proliferation treaty and on freezing North Korea's nuclear weapons programme.

There is also a big economic incentive for the United States to continue normal trade relations. U.S. officials estimate that 170,000 U.S. jobs depend on exports to China and that ending MFN could cost U.S. consumers $600 million a year in higher prices for shoes, clothing and appliances.
"The vote on MFN is a vote on how best to protect U.S. interests, not an endorsement of China's policies," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told reporters.

National Security Adviser Sandy Berger argued that to cut off MFN status to China would have little impact on Chinese policy, while diminishing future U.S. influence. "We are not going to isolate China, we are going to isolate ourselves from China. That is what this is about," he said.
